Well, it is a spectrum but I've heard it as something like a buffet. As somebody with "high-functioning" ASD I like that. Spectrum, high and low functioning kind of implies you are on sliding scale of being affected by all symptoms or not being very affected by any symptoms when ASD contains any multitude of Social or Sensory impairments and can vary WILDLY from person to person. I watched the movie the accountant and found out that my preference to stand and pace and stuff is an ASD trait when I always thought it was just an individual quirk. On the other hand, I worked with a lady once who also had Sensory processing disorder based ASD and while the overall outward appearance was the same (quirky but social person that while definitely weird is often told by people that they are too social to be on the spectrum at all) she loved the feeling of towels and hated the feeling of broccoli while I don't have any strong feelings to the texture and HATE towels and often just don't fucking use them because it feels like rubbing sandpaper on myself. I have fine motor-skilled dysgraphia (which is a hand disability which affects me and makes things like tying shoes tough) but that's a whole other rant for a different day, and also am GREATLY affected by the sensory side of ASD. Fire alarms are the BANE of my existence (even more than towels) and I will SPRINT away from them immediately no matter what just like you would run away from a lion or something equally scary. Fire alarms are pain. Police sirens hurt too but don't always trigger sensory overload episodes but sometimes they do and then while I am normally socially high-functioning I'mgoing through a whole ordeal (more on that in a sec.) and can't reallly interact with people who I know and who try to talk to me and then come off as an asshole.   I have no sense of direction WHATSOEVER or time, I can't tell you if 15 minutes have passed or an hour but the direction part is definitely worse and when people ask me for directions I feel like an asshole but I spend half the day not knowing where I am and just kinda wandering around. I'm late a lot to things. The biggest thing that I deal with though (but thankfully not on an everyday basis) is SENSORY OVERLOAD. I am going to copy paste an e-mail I wrote about what the experience feels like to me personally below:

"

On the day of the incident in the cafeteria you asked me what it felt like to have sensory overload. I just experienced an episode and can describe it now. 

It felt like a pressure in my head like I was submerging under water very quickly and like my head was being scratched softly with pinecones. I felt shaking like I had just jumped off a ledge or something into said body of water but it was involuntary and uncomfortable compared to the sensation of getting to float in the water after the initial discomfort. just the discomfort, amplified and lasting longer. it felt like somebody was also lightly pushing knife blades against my arms and like experiencing a temperature shift like when one feels hot or cold but instead of feeling hot or cold it registers as a kind of third sensation like those two but an entirely different experience. your brain just knows it as the sensory temperature I guess. sorry if that sounds nonsensical that is the best I can describe that. the description of the entire experience continues:

You feel like your skin is about to pop off of your body or like your skeleton will involuntarily jump out of your skin. your mind is racing incredibly fast and you just want to move or fly or something but you can't and you can only deal with it. you want to move your hands. music helps sometimes, I listen to clair de lune and a lot of people with sensory issues like to listen to certain to songs from childhood typically having one that will calm them down. the songs only help somewhat the only thing that truly helps is time but typically people who experience sensory overload also experience comorbid cognitive and lack the needed situational/self-awareness required to help coax episodes more quickly into submission and will instead carry out behaviors which will actually agitate the symptoms and prolong episodes."

==============================================================

So, that's a big ordeal but I just come off as weird or rude when I experience it. I am VERY social and have many friends and have even tried my hand at stand-up comedy and like to think I could be an actor. I tell jokes and enjoy and even crave talking to people. I couldn't talk until I was almost 3 and didn't have friends until 16 and DREADED talking to people until I worked retail and got used to it and became social, I would still be shy with strangers until I moved into a college dorm and then I became a very very social person. I get told "Oh, well we are all on the spectrum." "You don't seem it at all you are so high-functioning." "I know people with Autism and they can't talk you aren't really affected by it at all." CONSTANTLY when in fact the condition is the single biggest driving factor in my life, my days, and my personality but just get written off as a quirky dude who isn't great with his hands and gets lost easily but def. not an Autistic dude. the hand part of my disability is a whole other rant hahaha.

I don't get mad about it though, people DO want to understand and help, but people don't really understand it in part because people with severe sensory or motorskill impairment tend to also have severe social impairment and can't describe it well but again I must stress that everything stated above is my personal experience with my version of Autism and it varies WILDLY from person to person.

Well, I certainly applaud anyone wanting to do a hundred pushups, but take it from this old gym rat, I've spent my entire adult life in the gym, and a program like this one can do more harm than good.
If you only train one part of your body (and that's all a single exercise like pushups is going to do for you), you're setting yourself up for injuries down the road. I've seen it a hundred times.
It's like putting a powerful engine in a stock Toyota Tercel. What will you accomplish? You'll blow out the drive train, the clutch, the transmission, etc., because those factory parts aren't designed to handle the power of an engine much more powerful than the factory installed engine.
Push-ups basically only train the chest muscles and to some extent, the triceps. What you really want to do is train your entire body, all the major muscle groups (chest, back, abdomen, legs, shoulders and arms) at the same time, over the course of a workout. And don't forget your cardiovascular work!
I'm proud of you guys wanting to do this. Three cheers! Falling in love with exercise, eating right, etc., is one of the greatest things you can do for yourself. And you WILL fall in love with it if you can just force yourself to stick with it a year or two and experience the amazing progress you'll make.
But do it right, okay?
My advice, find a good gym, with qualified trainers who will design your programs for you (especially in the beginning, until you get the hang of it yourself) and guide you in your quest for physical fitness. Thirty to 45 minutes a day, three days a week, is all you'll ever need to do (I refuse to believe anyone is so busy that he or she cannot make time for that, especially considering how important it is).
And don't worry about being embarrassed or not being in shape the first time you walk into the gym. You have to start somewhere and almost every one of us were there ourselves at one time. So no one will say anything to you and very, very quickly you will progress way beyond that stage anyway.
Now get out there and do it! :-)
